members.name: of
members.summary:
Builds a Rational from one Integer over another.

This is the way to write a ratio of computed values, where the literal form `3/4` is not available. A zero denominator answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead.

entries.signature:
static of(
	_ numerator: Integer,
	over denominator: Integer,
) -> Optional<Rational>
entries.summary: Builds the Rational from two Integers, with nothing known about either.
entries.returns: the Rational, or nothing when the denominator is zero.

entries.signature: static of(_ numerator: Integer, over denominator: NonZeroInteger) -> Rational
entries.summary:
Builds the Rational over a denominator proven not to be zero.

There is no failure to report, so the Rational itself is the answer.

parameters.name: over
parameters.description: the denominator, proven not to be zero

entries.returns: the Rational.

entries.signature:
static of(
	_ numerator: Integer,
	over denominator: Integer,

entries.summary: Builds the Rational from two Integers, with a value to answer when the denominator is zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no Rational

entries.returns: the Rational, or the given value in its place.

members.name: parse
members.summary:
Reads a Rational from its text form.

The text is a fraction like `3/4`, a decimal like `0.75`, or a whole number like `3`. Each form takes an optional sign in front, and an underscore between two digits, which is the notation the language writes. Text of another shape, or a fraction over zero, answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead.

entries.returns: the Rational, or nothing when the text has any other shape or divides by zero.

entries.signature: static parse(_ text: String, defaultingTo fallback: Rational) -> Rational
entries.summary: Reads a Rational from its text form, with a value to answer when the text has another shape.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when the text is no Rational

entries.returns: the Rational, or the given value in its place.

members.name: is
members.summary:
Answers whether the Rational has the same value as a number.

The comparison is in lowest terms, so `1/2` equals `2/4`. A Rational equals an Integer when it is whole and its numerator is that Integer.

entries.summary: Answers whether the Rational has the same value as another Rational.
entries.returns: `true` when both are equal.

entries.summary: Answers whether the Rational has the same value as an Integer.
entries.returns: `true` when the Rational is whole and its numerator is that Integer.

members.name: isNot
members.summary:
Answers whether the Rational differs from a number.

A Rational that is not whole differs from every Integer.

entries.summary: Answers whether the Rational differs from another Rational.
entries.returns: `true` when the two differ.

entries.summary: Answers whether the Rational differs from an Integer.
entries.returns: `true` when the two differ.

entries.summary: Orders the Rational against another Rational.
entries.returns: `Ordering#Less`, `Ordering#Equal` or `Ordering#Greater`.

members.name: toString
members.summary:
Answers the Rational as a String, in lowest terms.

The form is `3/4` when no format is named, and the named format otherwise. A whole Rational prints its numerator alone, so `1/2::add(1/2)` prints `1` and `10::divide(by 2)` prints `5`. The `Rational.parse` Method reads the fraction form and the decimal form. The fraction form reads back as the same Rational. A decimal form does too when its expansion ends within 80 digits, and reads back as the rounded value otherwise. A count of one or more places writes exactly that many digits after the point.
members.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.summary:
Answers the Rational as a fraction, in lowest terms.

The form is `3/4`. A whole Rational prints its numerator alone, so `1/2::add(1/2)` prints `1`.
entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.summary:
Answers the Rational in the named format.

The `#Decimal` format writes the expansion, to at most 80 digits, and the `#Fraction` format writes `3/4`. A whole Rational prints its numerator alone in either. The `#Percent` format writes that same expansion of one hundred times the value, with a `%` after it. The `#Scientific` format writes one digit before the point and the power of ten as an exponent, so `1234` is `1.234e3` and zero is `0e0`.

parameters.name: as
parameters.description: the form to represent the Rational in

entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.signature:
toString(
	as format: NumberFormat,
	toPlaces count: Integer,
	toward direction: Rounding = #Nearest,
) -> String
entries.summary:
Answers the Rational in the named format, with exactly that many places.

The digits are padded with zeroes where the expansion is shorter, so `1/2` over two places is `0.50`. The last digit kept is rounded in the named direction, and `#Nearest` is what a call that names none is given, so `1/8` is `0.13`. A count below one rounds to a whole number, and no point is written. The count has no ceiling. The `#Percent` and `#Scientific` formats take the count the same way, so `1/8` over one place is `12.5%` and `1234` over two is `1.23e3`. The `#Fraction` format ignores both the count and the direction.

parameters.name: as
parameters.description: the form to represent the Rational in

parameters.name: toPlaces
parameters.description: how many digits to write after the point

parameters.name: toward
parameters.description: the direction to round the last digit in, `#Nearest` when it is left out

entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.signature: toString(as format: NumberFormat, groupingWith separator: String) -> String
entries.summary:
Answers the Rational in the named format, with a separator between the digit groups.

The separator goes between every three digits before the point, counted from the right, so `1234567` is `1,234,567` under a comma. The scientific form writes one digit before the point and takes no separator. The fraction form groups the numerator and the denominator alike.

parameters.name: as
parameters.description: the form to represent the Rational in

parameters.name: groupingWith
parameters.description: the text to write between the digit groups

entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.signature:
toString(
	as format: NumberFormat,
	toPlaces count: Integer,
	groupingWith separator: String,
	toward direction: Rounding = #Nearest,
) -> String
entries.summary:
Answers the Rational in the named format, with that many places and a separator between the digit groups.

The count and the direction reach the format exactly as they do without a separator, so `1234567/1` over two places is `1,234,567.00` under a comma. Only the digits before the point are grouped.

parameters.name: as
parameters.description: the form to represent the Rational in

parameters.name: toPlaces
parameters.description: how many digits to write after the point

parameters.name: groupingWith
parameters.description: the text to write between the digit groups

parameters.name: toward
parameters.description: the direction to round the last digit in, `#Nearest` when it is left out

entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

entries.summary:
Answers the Rational as a fraction, with its sign written in the named style.

The `#Always` Case writes a `+` in front of a value that is not negative, so `3/4` is `+3/4` and zero is `+0`. The `#Negative` Case writes what the plain `toString()` writes.

parameters.name: showingSign
parameters.description: whether to write a sign in front of a value that is not negative

entries.returns: the String representation of the Rational.

members.name: add
members.summary: Adds a number to the Rational, and stays exact for every member of the numeric tower.

entries.returns: the sum.

entries.summary:
Adds an Integer to the Rational.

The sum is a Rational, since a whole number added to a fraction need not be whole.
entries.returns: the sum, as a Rational.

entries.summary:
Adds an Algebraic to the Rational.

The sum is an Algebraic, since adding a Rational leaves the radical part in place.
entries.returns: the sum, as an Algebraic.

entries.summary:
Adds a Transcendental to the Rational.

The sum is a Transcendental, since adding a Rational leaves every base term in place.
entries.returns: the sum, as a Transcendental.

members.name: add
members.summary:
Adds a Rational proven not to be negative to this NonNegativeRational.

A sum of two non-negative Rationals is never negative, and a positive summand makes it positive.

entries.summary:
Adds a Rational proven to be positive.

The receiver is not negative and the other summand is above zero, so the sum is above zero.
entries.returns: the sum, which is above zero.

entries.summary:
Adds a Rational proven not to be negative.

Neither summand is negative, so the sum is not negative either.
entries.returns: the sum, which is never negative.

entries.summary:
Adds a Rational proven not to be negative to this PositiveRational.

The receiver is above zero and the other summand is not below it, so the sum is above zero.
entries.returns: the sum, which is above zero.

members.name: subtract
members.summary: Subtracts a number from the Rational, and stays exact for every member of the numeric tower.

entries.returns: the difference.

entries.summary:
Subtracts an Integer from the Rational.

The difference is a Rational, since a whole number taken from a fraction need not be whole.
entries.returns: the difference, as a Rational.

entries.summary:
Subtracts an Algebraic from the Rational.

The difference is an Algebraic, since the radical part stays and only its sign flips.
entries.returns: the difference, as an Algebraic.

entries.summary:
Subtracts a Transcendental from the Rational.

The difference is a Transcendental, since every base term stays with its sign flipped.
entries.returns: the difference, as a Transcendental.

members.name: multiply
members.summary: Multiplies the Rational with a number, and stays exact for every member of the numeric tower.

entries.returns: the product.

entries.summary:
Multiplies the Rational with an Integer.

The product is a Rational, since scaling a fraction by a whole number need not leave a whole number.
entries.returns: the product, as a Rational.

entries.summary:
Multiplies the Rational with an Algebraic.

The product is an Algebraic, since scaling keeps the radical part. A zero receiver answers zero, which is a Rational.
entries.returns: the product, as an Algebraic or a Rational.

entries.summary:
Multiplies the Rational with a Transcendental.

The product is a Transcendental, since scaling keeps every base term. A zero receiver answers zero, which is a Rational.
entries.returns: the product, as a Transcendental or a Rational.

entries.summary:
Multiplies this NonZeroRational with another.

The product is never zero, so the answer is a NonZeroRational too.
entries.returns: the product, which is not zero.

entries.summary:
Multiplies this NonNegativeRational with a Rational proven not to be negative.

Neither factor is negative, so the product is not negative either.
entries.returns: the product, which is never negative.

entries.summary:
Multiplies this PositiveRational with another.

Both factors are above zero, so the product is above zero.
entries.returns: the product, which is above zero.

members.name: divide
members.summary:
Divides the Rational by a number, exactly.

Dividing by an Integer or a Rational answers empty for a zero divisor. With `defaultingTo`, the given value stands in place of empty. Dividing by an Algebraic always answers, because an Algebraic is irrational and so never zero. Dividing by an Integer proven not to be zero always answers too. A Rational proven not to be zero answers as well.

entries.returns: the quotient, or nothing when the divisor is zero.

entries.summary:
Divides the Rational by an Integer.

The quotient is a Rational. A zero divisor answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead.
entries.returns: the quotient, or nothing when the divisor is zero.

entries.summary:
Divides the Rational by an Algebraic.

An Algebraic is irrational and so never zero, which is why the quotient itself is the answer. The quotient is an Algebraic, and a zero receiver answers zero, which is a Rational.
entries.returns: the quotient, as an Algebraic or a Rational.

entries.signature: divide(by other: Rational, defaultingTo fallback: Rational) -> Rational
entries.summary: Divides by a Rational, and answers the given value when the divisor is zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no quotient

entries.returns: the quotient, or the given value in its place.

entries.signature: divide(by other: Integer, defaultingTo fallback: Rational) -> Rational
entries.summary: Divides by an Integer, and answers the given value when the divisor is zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no quotient

entries.returns: the quotient, or the given value in its place.

entries.summary:
Divides by an Integer proven not to be zero.

There is no failure to report, so the quotient itself is the answer.

parameters.name: by
parameters.description: the divisor, proven not to be zero

entries.returns: the quotient.

entries.summary:
Divides by a Rational proven not to be zero.

There is no failure to report, so the quotient itself is the answer.

parameters.name: by
parameters.description: the divisor, proven not to be zero

entries.returns: the quotient.

members.name: remainder
members.summary:
Answers what is left over after taking out every whole divisor that fits.

The division is Euclidean, so the remainder is never negative and always below the divisor's magnitude. For example, `7/2::remainder(dividingBy 1/3)` is `1/6`. A zero divisor answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead.

entries.summary: Answers the remainder over a divisor nothing is known about.
entries.returns: the remainder, or nothing when dividing by zero.

entries.summary:
Answers the remainder over a divisor proven not to be zero.

The division can not fail, so the answer is the remainder itself rather than an Optional.

parameters.name: dividingBy
parameters.description: the divisor, proven not to be zero

entries.returns: the remainder.

entries.signature:
remainder(
	dividingBy divisor: Rational,
	defaultingTo fallback: Rational,
) -> Rational
entries.summary: Answers the remainder, with a value to answer when the divisor is zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no remainder

entries.returns: the remainder, or the given value in its place.

members.name: quotient
members.summary:
Answers how many whole divisors fit.

This is the other half of the same Euclidean division as `remainder`, and the two agree: `quotient · divisor + remainder` is the original Rational. For example, `7/2::quotient(dividingBy 1/3)` is `10`. A zero divisor answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Integer instead.

entries.summary: Answers the quotient over a divisor nothing is known about.
entries.returns: the quotient, or nothing when dividing by zero.

entries.summary:
Answers the quotient over a divisor proven not to be zero.

The division can not fail, so the answer is the quotient itself rather than an Optional.

parameters.name: dividingBy
parameters.description: the divisor, proven not to be zero

entries.returns: the quotient.

entries.signature:
quotient(
	dividingBy divisor: Rational,
	defaultingTo fallback: Integer,
) -> Integer
entries.summary: Answers the quotient, with a value to answer when the divisor is zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no quotient

entries.returns: the quotient, or the given value in its place.

members.name: raise
members.summary:
Raises the Rational to the given power.

A negative exponent answers the exact reciprocal power. Zero raised to the power of zero is one. Raising this Rational to an exponent proven not to be negative can not fail. Zero raised to a negative power answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead.

entries.returns: the power, or nothing when raising zero to a negative power.

entries.signature:
raise(
	to exponent: Integer,
	defaultingTo fallback: Rational,
) -> Rational
entries.summary: Raises the Rational to the given power, and answers the given value when there is no power.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no power

entries.returns: the power, or the given value in its place.

entries.summary:
Raises the Rational to an exponent proven not to be negative.

Every Rational has such a power, the reciprocal is never taken, and no denominator can reach zero. So the answer is the power itself rather than an Optional.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: the exponent, proven not to be negative

entries.returns: the power.

members.name: squareRoot
members.summary:
Answers the exact square root of the Rational.

A perfect square answers a Rational. Any other value that is not negative answers an exact Algebraic. A negative Rational answers empty, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given value instead.

entries.returns: the root, or nothing for a negative Rational.

entries.summary: Answers the exact square root, with a value to answer for a negative Rational.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no root

entries.returns: the root, or the given value in its place.

entries.summary:
Answers the exact square root of this NonNegativeRational.

A negative Rational is the one with no real root, and the receiver is proven not to be one. So the answer is the root itself rather than an Optional. A ratio of two perfect squares answers a Rational, and every other value answers an exact Algebraic.
entries.returns: the root.

entries.summary:
Answers the exact square root of this PositiveRational.

A ratio of two perfect squares above zero has a root above zero, and every other value answers an exact Algebraic.
entries.returns: the root.

members.name: isLessThan
members.summary: Answers whether the Rational is strictly below the given number.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is strictly below another Rational.

The comparison is in lowest terms, so `1/2` is not below `2/4`.
entries.returns: `true` when the receiver is below the other Rational.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is strictly below an Integer.

The Integer is read as `n/1`, so `1/2` is below `1`.
entries.returns: `true` when the Rational is below the Integer.

members.name: isLessThanOrEqualTo
members.summary: Answers whether the Rational is below the given number, or equal to it.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is below another Rational, or equal to it.

Equal Rationals answer `true`.
The comparison is in lowest terms, so `1/2` answers `true` against `2/4`.
entries.returns: `true` when the receiver is below the other Rational or equal to it.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is below an Integer, or equal to it.

The Integer is read as `n/1`, so `2/2` answers `true` against `1`.
entries.returns: `true` when the Rational is below the Integer or equal to it.

members.name: isGreaterThan
members.summary: Answers whether the Rational is strictly above the given number.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is strictly above another Rational.

The comparison is in lowest terms, so `2/4` is not above `1/2`.
entries.returns: `true` when the receiver is above the other Rational.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is strictly above an Integer.

The Integer is read as `n/1`, so `3/2` is above `1`.
entries.returns: `true` when the Rational is above the Integer.

members.name: isGreaterThanOrEqualTo
members.summary: Answers whether the Rational is above the given number, or equal to it.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is above another Rational, or equal to it.

Equal Rationals answer `true`.
The comparison is in lowest terms, so `2/4` answers `true` against `1/2`.
entries.returns: `true` when the receiver is above the other Rational or equal to it.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is above an Integer, or equal to it.

The Integer is read as `n/1`, so `2/2` answers `true` against `1`.
entries.returns: `true` when the Rational is above the Integer or equal to it.

entries.signature: isBetween(_ lower: Rational, and upper: Rational) -> Boolean
entries.summary:
Answers whether the value lies between the two given ones, both included.

The two bounds name the same range in either order: `7::isBetween(10, and 1)` is `true`, and `15::isBetween(10, and 1)` is `false`.

parameters.description: one bound of the range, included

parameters.name: and
parameters.description: the other bound of the range, included

entries.returns: `true` when the value is within the bounds.

entries.signature: clamp(between lowest: Rational, and highest: Rational) -> Rational
entries.summary:
Answers the value, pulled into the given bounds.

The answer is the lower bound when the value is below it. It is the upper bound when the value is above it, and the value itself otherwise. The two bounds name the same range in either order: `7::clamp(between 10, and 1)` is `7`, and `15::clamp(between 10, and 1)` is `10`.

parameters.name: and
parameters.description: the other bound of the range

entries.returns: the clamped value.

entries.summary:
Answers whether the Rational is a whole number.

A whole number has the denominator one in lowest terms.

Answers whether the Rational is above zero.

Zero is neither positive nor negative.

Answers whether the Rational is below zero.

Zero is neither positive nor negative.
Answers whether the Rational is exactly zero.

Answers the numerator of the Rational in lowest terms.

The numerator carries the sign, because the denominator is always positive.

Answers the numerator of this NonZeroRational in lowest terms.

A Rational is zero exactly when its numerator is, and the receiver is proven not to be zero. So the answer is a NonZeroInteger.
entries.returns: the numerator, which is not zero.

entries.summary:
Answers the denominator of the Rational in lowest terms.

The denominator is always positive, and never zero. So the answer is a PositiveInteger, which fits every position that asks for a NonZeroInteger or a NonNegativeInteger.
Answers the Rational without its sign, which is its distance from zero.
entries.returns: the distance, which is never negative.

entries.summary:
Answers this NonZeroRational without its sign, which is its distance from zero.

The receiver is not zero, so its distance from zero is above zero. So the answer is a PositiveRational.
entries.returns: the distance, which is above zero.

entries.summary: Answers the Rational with its sign flipped.

Answers this NonZeroRational with its sign flipped.

Negation keeps a value away from zero, so the answer is a NonZeroRational too.
entries.returns: the negation, which is not zero.

members.name: reciprocal
members.summary:
Answers the reciprocal of the Rational.

The reciprocal exchanges the numerator and the denominator. Zero has no reciprocal, and the `defaultingTo:` entry answers the given Rational instead. A receiver proven not to be zero answers the reciprocal itself.

entries.returns: the reciprocal, or nothing for zero.

entries.summary: Answers the reciprocal, with a value to answer for zero.

parameters.name: defaultingTo
parameters.description: the value to answer with when there is no reciprocal

entries.returns: the reciprocal, or the given value in its place.

entries.summary:
Answers the reciprocal of this NonZeroRational.

Zero is the one Rational with no reciprocal, and the receiver is proven not to be one. So the answer is the reciprocal itself rather than an Optional. Exchanging the two parts of a value that is not zero leaves a value that is not zero, so the answer is proven as well.
entries.returns: the reciprocal, which is not zero.

members.name: round
members.summary:
Answers the Rational rounded in the named direction.

The direction is `#Nearest` when a call names none. A value exactly halfway between two steps rounds away from zero, so `1/2` answers `1` and `-1/2` answers `-1`. Under `#NearestEven` a value exactly halfway between two steps reaches the even one, so `1/2` answers `0` and `3/2` answers `2`. The other directions answer the floor for `#Down`, the ceiling for `#Up`, and the value towards zero for `#TowardZero`. Naming a count of places rounds to a decimal grid of that width instead, and answers a Rational.

entries.summary: Answers the Rational as an Integer, rounded in the named direction.

parameters.name: toward
parameters.description: the direction to round in, `#Nearest` when it is left out

entries.returns: the rounded Integer.

entries.signature:
round(
	toPlaces places: Integer,
	toward direction: Rounding = #Nearest,
) -> Rational
entries.summary:
Answers the Rational rounded to a decimal grid of the given width.

Two places round to hundredths, so `5/3` answers `167/100`. The answer is exact, and it is a Rational rather than text: `toString(as #Decimal, toPlaces 2)` is what writes `1.67`. A count below one rounds to a whole number, answered as a Rational. The count has no ceiling, as it has none on `toString`.

parameters.name: toPlaces
parameters.description: how many decimal places to keep

parameters.name: toward
parameters.description: the direction to round in, `#Nearest` when it is left out

entries.returns: the rounded Rational.

entries.signature:
approximate(
	toPlaces places: NonNegativeInteger,
	toward direction: Rounding = #Nearest,
) -> Rational
entries.summary:
Answers the Rational read off a decimal grid of the given width.

A Rational is exact, so the answer is the same one `round(toPlaces:toward:)` gives: two places answer hundredths, and `5/3` answers `167/100`. The entries of this name on `Algebraic` and on `Transcendental` are what make an irrational readable as a number. This one is what lets a `Number` receiver reach the family.

parameters.name: toPlaces
parameters.description: how many decimal places to keep

parameters.name: toward
parameters.description: the direction to round in, `#Nearest` when it is left out

entries.returns: the Rational on that grid.

entries.summary:
Answers the Rational as a Rational.

A Rational is one already, so the answer is the receiver itself. The entry is what lets a `Scalar` receiver reach the crossing that an Integer receiver reaches.
entries.returns: the receiver itself.

refinements.name: NonZeroRational
refinements.description:
The Rationals that are not zero, as a checked refinement of `Rational`, and the sister of `NonZeroInteger`.

The proof is what lets `reciprocal` answer a Rational rather than an Optional. The `numerator` is a NonZeroInteger, and `absolute`, `negate` and multiplication answer one of these again.

refinements.name: NonNegativeRational
refinements.description:
The Rationals from zero upward, as a checked refinement of `Rational`.

A receiver proven to be one of these has a real square root, which the bare `squareRoot` answers an Optional for. Addition and multiplication stay within the proof.

refinements.name: PositiveRational
refinements.description:
The Rationals above zero, as a checked refinement of `Rational`.

A value above zero is neither zero nor below it, so one of these is accepted wherever a NonZeroRational or a NonNegativeRational is wanted. Addition with a value that is not negative, and multiplication with another of these, answer one of these again.

modes.name: NumberFormat
modes.description:
The forms `Rational::toString` writes: `#Fraction` is `"3/4"`, `#Decimal` is `"0.75"`, `#Percent` is `"75%"` and `#Scientific` is `"7.5e-1"`.

The plain `toString()` entry writes the fraction form, and the `as:` entries name one of the four. The scientific form writes one digit before the point, and the power of ten it took out as `e` and an exponent. Only the fraction form and the decimal form read back through `Rational.parse`.

modes.name: Rounding
modes.declaration:
choice Rounding {
	Nearest,
	NearestEven,
	Down,
	Up,
	TowardZero,
}
modes.description:
Which step `round` reaches for a value that is not already on one.

`#Nearest` goes to the closest step, and away from zero for a value exactly halfway between two. The `#NearestEven` Case goes to the closest step as well. A value exactly halfway between two steps reaches the even one of them. The `#Down` Case answers the floor, `#Up` the ceiling, and `#TowardZero` the step towards zero. A call that names no rounding gets `#Nearest`.

modes.name: SignStyle
modes.description:
Whether `toString(showingSign:)` writes a sign in front of a value that is not negative.

A negative value is written with its minus sign under both Cases. Under `#Always` a value that is not negative is written with a `+` in front, and zero is `+0`. A call that names `#Negative` gets what the plain `toString()` writes.
